items.label: Direct-lending default rate (%, Fitch incl. distressed exchanges)
items.rationale: Fitch's broad-definition PCDR (inclusive measure counting distressed exchanges and maturity extensions) printed 6.3% TTM through August 2026, a new record high surpassing the prior 6.1% in July; this is the controlling Fitch reading per the rubric and displaces the April 6.0% anchor. The rate has been above 6% continuously since April 2026 with August producing 14 default events—the highest monthly count in the trailing-year window—corroborating persistent middle-market credit stress.
items.fact: Fitch Ratings reported the trailing 12-month US private credit default rate (inclusive of distressed exchanges and liability-management exercises, across ~1,300-1,500 borrowers) rose to 6.3% at end-August 2026, up from 6.1% in July and a prior record of 6.0% in April-May 2026. Source: Bloomberg, 14 Sep 2026 (https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-14/us-private-credit-default-rate-hits-a-record-of-6-3-fitch-says); corroborated by Newsbreak/Benzinga and Epoch Times citing the same Fitch release.

dissent.view: Proskauer Private Credit Default Index: 2.51% in Q2 2026 (count-based, senior secured/unitranche, 716 loans, $195.6B). Materially lower due to narrower coverage and exclusion of many distressed-exchange events.
Moody's: 2025 private credit headline default rate 1.6%-4.7% excluding distressed restructurings; estimated ~65% of 2025 defaults were distressed exchanges/maturity extensions.

items.label: GENIUS implementation friction (0 smooth / 1 gaps / 2 problems)
items.rationale: The rubric's Level 2 condition is 'deadline missed without final rules': the July 18, 2026 statutory deadline has passed with zero final rules promulgated across all seven required agencies, confirmed by multiple authoritative trackers as of September 2026. No court stay is needed to score 2 — the plain missed-deadline-without-final-rules criterion is fully satisfied.
items.fact: The statutory July 18, 2026 deadline for GENIUS Act implementing final rules was missed by all seven required agencies (OCC, FDIC, Federal Reserve, NCUA, Treasury, FinCEN, OFAC). As of early September 2026, 'not a single final rule' has been issued across any of the 10 NPRMs filed, per the Chapman & Cutler rulemaking tracker and confirmed by Yahoo Finance/ABA Banking Journal (Sept 2026). The OCC Comptroller publicly committed to a final rule 'by November' at the Wyoming Blockchain Symposium on Aug 19, 2026. Treasury's NPRM on issuance/offer/sale was published Aug 18, 2026, with comments due Oct 19, 2026 — structurally precluding finalization before that date. Source: fdic.gov (Apr 7 2026 NPRM); federalregister.gov (Aug 18 2026 Treasury NPRM); yahoo.com/finance 'GENIUS Act Compliance Cliff' (early Sept 2026); chapman.com tracker (as of Jul 16 2026); occ.gov Bulletin 2026-3.

dissent.view: Some sources (Chapman & Cutler tracker, Paradigm tracker) note agencies frequently miss statutory deadlines with limited practical consequences and that the Jan 18, 2027 effective date backstop remains operative, implying the overall framework is not in crisis — suggesting a softer read closer to '1' (gaps) rather than hard failure.

tech-insider.org characterises the situation as 'every major package still stuck at the proposal stage' but frames it as an administrative sequencing issue rather than a systemic breakdown, which could support a '1' (gaps) classification.

items.label: Large-fund redemption gates (0 none / 1 isolated / 2 widespread)
items.rationale: The rubric's level-2 threshold (>=3 of the largest funds gating, or combined AUM >$100bn) is far exceeded: 10 of 16 tracked BDCs hit their caps in the same quarter (Q2 2026), with BCRED alone at ~$79bn AUM and multiple other multi-billion-dollar funds (Ares, Apollo, Blue Owl, Morgan Stanley, Oaktree) simultaneously gating. No corroborating funding-market signal is required to override — the breadth (majority of Fitch's sample) and named-fund AUM aggregation well above $100bn makes this unambiguously WIDESPREAD.
items.fact: Fitch Ratings data (reported August 2026) shows 10 of 16 tracked non-traded BDCs breached their quarterly 5% repurchase caps in Q2 2026, with total redemption requests of $15.6 billion unfulfilled. Named funds enforcing gates include: Blackstone Private Credit Fund (BCRED, ~$79bn AUM, ~10% Q2 requests vs 5% cap), Ares Strategic Income Fund (14.4% Q2 requests, capped at 5%), Apollo Debt Solutions BDC (17% Q2 requests, capped at 5%), Blue Owl OBDC II ($1.6bn, repurchase program fully suspended in Feb 2026), Morgan Stanley North Haven Private Income Fund (11.6% Q2 requests), and Oaktree Strategic Credit Fund (6.8% Q1 requests, cap expanded). Sources: Fitch Ratings via angelinvestorsnetwork.com (Aug 20 2026); alternativecreditinvestor.com (Jun 27 2026); abfjournal.com (May 28 2026); altswire.com (May 17 2026).

dissent.view: Some analysts (CAIA, iCapital, CLA) characterise gate activation as 'funds operating as designed' rather than a stress event, noting gates are contractual features not credit deterioration signals, and that early Q3 2026 data (e.g. Golub GCRED cleared July tender in full at 4.8%) suggests possible peak.

items.label: AI capex-vs-revenue gap concern (0 closing / 1 wide / 2 widening fast)
items.rationale: Capex growth (~77% YoY aggregate) materially exceeds cloud/AI-revenue growth (37-82% YoY by segment, but starting from a far smaller base — AI run rates still lag full capex by a wide margin per io-fund.com). However, all three major cloud units accelerated QoQ (Google Cloud: 63%->82%; AWS: 28%->37%; Azure: ~40%->43%), ruling out the QoQ deceleration or guidance-cut trigger required for a score of 2; the gap is wide but not widening on the revenue-momentum dimension, placing this squarely at rubric level 1.

Meanwhile aggregate 2026 capex guidance was simultaneously raised: Amazon to ~$220B, Alphabet to $195-205B, Meta to $130-145B — combined ~$740-760B, up ~77% from ~$410B in 2025. Sources: fourweekmba.com citing Amazon/Alphabet/Microsoft Q2 2026 earnings releases; uncoveralpha.com citing Q2 2026 earnings; kucoin.com citing Alphabet Q2 2026 earnings (July 31 2026).

bingx.com (Jul 31 2026) reports Amazon trailing-twelve-month FCF turned negative (-$7.6B) and Meta FCF fell 91%, framing the capex-versus-cash-conversion gap as a near-term financing risk rather than a pure revenue-momentum story.

items.label: Insurer non-renewals / exits (0 stable / 1 rising / 2 accelerating)
items.rationale: Non-renewal waves are documented across all four NAIC regions with at least 7 named states experiencing elevated non-renewals/partial exits - firmly in the 5-15 state RISING band - but the NAIC characterizes the national market as 'operationally strong overall' with improved 2024 underwriting results and no confirmed top-10 insurer full-state exit in 2026, precluding the ACCELERATING threshold of >15 states or a full top-10 exit.
items.fact: NAIC's August 5, 2026 first-of-its-kind MCAS report ('Examining Homeowner Property Insurance Market Dynamics: An Assessment of Countrywide State-Level Data From 2018 to 2024') found company-initiated non-renewal rates rose 96%-216% across ALL FOUR U.S. geographic regions (Northeast, Southeast, Midwest, West) from 2018-2024, with the steepest increases in the West (>3x). The Southeast region showed a continuous net decline in carrier count across the full 7-year period (-4%). Florida non-renewed 3.35% of policies in 2024 (highest nationally, 1.7x 2018 rate); California non-renewed 3.18% (3.9x its 2018 rate). Named states with active non-renewal/exit stress include CA, FL, LA, TX, CO, GA, OK - at minimum 7 states per contemporaneous reporting (Insurance Journal, rollingout.com, climatecosmos.com). The market is described as 'overall operationally robust but nonetheless under pressure and exhibiting signs of stress.' No confirmed full exit of a top-10 insurer from an entire major state in 2026; Citizens FL policy count fell from 1.42M (Oct 2023) to ~385K-395K (Jan 2026) showing private-market re-entry in FL. (Primary source: NAIC MCAS report, naic.org, Aug 5 2026; supporting: CNBC Aug 6 2026, beinsure.com Aug 12 2026)

dissent.view: S&P Global Market Intelligence shows U.S. effective approved homeowners rate change collapsed to just 1.8% through July 2026 (from 13.6% in 2024), suggesting material market stabilization that could argue toward STABLE in some geographies
Climate Cosmos (June 2026) lists 13 named states with active non-renewal drops, which if treated as a discrete state count would approach or exceed the ACCELERATING rubric threshold of >15

items.label: Regional-bank CRE stress (0 calm / 1 isolated / 2 cluster)
items.rationale: With 1-2 failures in the trailing 6-month window where FDIC/credible sources explicitly cite CRE/real-estate exposure as a contributing factor (Metropolitan Capital via FDIC OIG May 2026, Community Bank & Trust-West Georgia via FDIC enforcement action), and all failures well below $10B with no interagency CRE emergency action, the rubric maps to ISOLATED (score=1). The broader 4-failure count in the window does not clear the CLUSTER bar because CRE is only explicitly attributed to 1-2 of them, with reporting characterizing the pattern as idiosyncratic community bank operating failures rather than a CRE-driven systemic event.
items.fact: Five US banks failed in 2026 YTD per FDIC (fdic.gov/resources/resolutions/bank-failures/in-brief/2026): Metropolitan Capital Bank & Trust (Jan 30, $261M assets, CRE/real-estate loan exposure documented by FDIC OIG review dated May 29 2026 and Bisnow reporting); Community Bank and Trust-West Georgia (May 1, $288M assets, preceded by FDIC enforcement action April 2026); Kentland FSL (July, tiny); Small Business Bank Lenexa KS (July, ~$73M); Tioga-Franklin Savings Bank (Aug 21, $68M). In the trailing 6 months (Mar 21-Sep 21 2026), 4 failures occurred. Of these, 1-2 have CRE/real-estate exposure explicitly cited as a contributing factor; the remainder are attributed to general capital erosion and operating deficiencies. No failure exceeded $10B in assets and no coordinated interagency CRE-specific supervisory action was identified.

items.label: Large public-pension funded ratio (%)
items.rationale: The Milliman PPFI is the canonical monthly mark-to-market index for the 100 largest U.S. public pensions, directly satisfying the rubric; 88.2 is the most recently published figure as of the research date. Equable Institute's broader FY2026 projection of 85.0% covers 253 systems including smaller, weaker plans, explaining the ~3pp gap.

items.label: New IMF programs / missed coupons (0 calm / 1 rising / 2 cluster)
items.rationale: Ukraine's new EFF (approved Feb 26 2026, active throughout the window) plus Argentina's ongoing EFF (review milestone May 2026) constitute 1-2 newly active IMF arrangements with no confirmed missed coupons, mapping to RISING (band 1); no evidence of >=3 sovereigns in new programs or default supports ruling out CLUSTER (band 2).
items.fact: IMF Executive Board approved a new US$8.1 billion 48-month EFF for Ukraine on Feb 26 2026 (source: imf.org/en/news/articles/2026/02/26/pr-26066-ukraine); Argentina operates under a US$20-21bn EFF agreed in 2025 with a review cleared May 2026 (source: batimes.com.ar, May 22 2026); no confirmed new sovereign missed coupons or fresh defaults found in the Mar-Sep 2026 window.

dissent.view: Ukraine EFF approval date (Feb 26 2026) falls just outside the strict trailing-6-month window (Mar 21 - Sep 21 2026), which could reduce the count to ~1 (Argentina continuation only) and support CALM (0)

items.label: Reserve-weaponization / settlement shift (0 none / 1 talk / 2 action)
items.rationale: The formal adoption of BRICS Pay at the New Delhi Declaration (Sep 12, 2026) and the BRICS Unit pilot constitute new non-dollar settlement agreements and launches, squarely mapping to rubric level 1 (TALK/agreements). No new sovereign reserve freeze or operationally transformative reserve settlement shift by a major economy has been confirmed, so the evidence does not reach level 2.
items.fact: At the 18th BRICS Summit (New Delhi, 12-13 Sep 2026), leaders adopted the New Delhi Declaration formally endorsing BRICS Pay - 'a decentralized payment messaging ecosystem designed to route cross-border transactions through national systems rather than the dollar-denominated SWIFT network' - and addressed the gold-backed BRICS Unit token pilot; crucially, 'BRICS Pay is not a currency and does not replace the dollar as a reserve asset' (Eastern Herald, 12 Sep 2026). No new sovereign reserve seizure occurred: Russian assets remain frozen under the pre-existing 2022 G7/EU freeze, with EU permanent-seizure proposals still debated but not enacted as of Sep 2026 (Brookings, Jun 2025; CFR, Nov 2025).

dissent.view: Some sources (informedclearly.com, watcher.guru) characterise BRICS Pay as already 'operational' and claim intra-bloc local-currency trade has surpassed 67%, suggesting a more advanced de-dollarisation that could edge toward ACTION; however these are non-primary, speculative outlets and the New Delhi Declaration language and RBI/EBC reporting confirm BRICS Pay remains a payment messaging layer, not a reserve settlement system replacement.

items.label: Social Security / pension reform shock (0 none / 1 debate / 2 cuts)
items.rationale: The trustees report worsened the depletion date (2033 -> 2032) and the 75-year actuarial deficit widened to 4.42% of taxable payroll, squarely satisfying rubric band 1 (depletion date worsened, reform actively debated). No automatic cut has been triggered and no legislation enacting cuts has been signed, so band 2 is not met.
items.fact: The 2026 Social Security Trustees Report (released June 9, 2026; primary source: ssa.gov/oact/trsum/) projects OASI trust fund depletion in Q4 2032 -- one quarter earlier than the prior report -- with only 78% of scheduled benefits payable thereafter. No legislation enacting benefit cuts or restoring solvency has been enacted; multiple bills (Bipartisan Social Security Commission Act H.R. 9187, PROMISE Act introduced July 14, 2026) are proposed but none passed.

dissent.view: AARP/CRS report combined OASDI depletion unchanged at 2034 (Q3 2034), framing the headline as 'no change' vs. the OASI-only 2032 worsening; the distinction is real but both readings confirm no enacted cuts.

items.label: USD share of FX reserves (%, IMF COFER)
items.rationale: The rubric calls for the latest USD share of allocated global FX reserves as a percent; the IMF COFER 2026Q1 release is the most recent official quarterly publication, reporting exactly 57.13%. This maps directly and mechanically to the indicator with no ambiguity.
items.fact: IMF COFER Data Brief (data.imf.org, published 2026-06-30): 'The share of US dollar holdings in foreign exchange reserves increased to 57.13 percent in 2026Q1, from 56.42 percent in 2025Q4.'

dissent.view: coferdata.com tracker displays USD share at 56.77%, consistent with the prior 2025Q4 IMF release (Mar 27 2026 brief), not the latest 2026Q1 figure

items.label: Ex-China heavy rare-earth price premium (x China)
items.rationale: Dividing the mid-point ex-China dysprosium price (~$1,100/kg) by the China domestic reference (~$215/kg) yields ~5.1x, consistent with the 4-5x range reported by multiple sources as of mid-to-late September 2026; the rubric asks for the approximate multiple, so 5.0 is the best single reading.
items.fact: China domestic dysprosium oxide ~$212-218/kg (CREIA index 262.0, Sept 17 2026); ex-China (USA Rare Earth indicative) ~$1,100/kg; Rare Earth Exchanges (Sept 17 2026) headline: 'dysprosium and terbium prices outside China can run 4-5x higher.' Argus data cited by Reuters (June 2026) also reports Dy/Tb ex-China at x4-x5. Benchmark Minerals (March 24 2026) pegged 2025 avg at 4.4x CIF N. America, trending higher through 2026.

dissent.view: Metal.com/SMM H1 2026 review characterises heavy REE ex-China premium as only '30-40% over domestic Chinese levels' — far below all other sources and likely reflects FOB vs domestic spread rather than true CIF ex-China Western-buyer premium
Benchmark Minerals forecasts the multiple rising to 8.3x by 2027, implying the current 2026 reading is still in transition above the 4.4x 2025 baseline but not yet at the forecast peak

items.label: New tariff/anti-dumping actions (0 calm / 1 rising / 2 escalating)
items.rationale: The rubric scores ESCALATING (2) at >=4 new measures OR a broad tariff round >=10% across a sector; the trailing 3 months produced at least 5 discrete measures including the 12.5% US Section 301 forced-labor tariff (a broad cross-sector round), EU sector-specific AD duties, and Chinese retaliatory export controls, clearly clearing both thresholds.
items.fact: In the trailing 3 months: (1) USTR imposed a new 12.5% Section 301 forced-labor tariff on Chinese goods effective 24 July 2026 (China Briefing, 23 Jul 2026); (2) EU imposed definitive AD duties of 4.3%-45.3% on Chinese car/lorry tyres, 7 Jul 2026 (EC trade policy page); (3) EU raised ceramic tableware AD duties on China to 79% (amfori.org); (4) China expanded rare earth export controls to 10 US firms 22 Jun 2026 and 14 EU firms 24 Jul 2026 (tech-insider.org/MOFCOM); (5) China introduced drone export controls and entity sanctions 5 Aug 2026 (usahousinginformation.com). Total: >=5 new distinct measures across multiple major economies.

dissent.view: CRS (Aug 18 2026) frames the US-China relationship as still inside a managed negotiating track with trade/investment boards created in May 2026, suggesting escalation is bounded rather than open-ended.

items.label: Nov-2025 pause status (0 extended / 1 expiring / 2 lapsed)
items.rationale: The truce is <90 days from expiry with no confirmed renewal, and partial breaches (new entity-list additions to MP Materials/USA Rare Earth, Japan rare-earth ban) have been formally flagged by the US — squarely meeting the rubric's '1 = EXPIRING/fraying' threshold. Score 2 is not warranted because the suspension itself has not formally lapsed and controls have not been reimposed on US-bound shipments.
items.fact: China's one-year suspension of Oct-9-2025 rare-earth export controls remains nominally in force but expires November 10, 2026 — under 51 days away with no renewal announced. China added 10 US firms (incl. MP Materials, USA Rare Earth) to restrictions in June 2026 (Reuters) and maintains a rare-earth export ban on Japan which the US formally contests as a truce breach (NPR, 2026-09-17). Trump-Xi Washington summit to discuss renewal is scheduled for Sept 24. Source: The National News, 2026-09-21; NPR, 2026-09-17; Modern Diplomacy, 2026-08-21.

dissent.view: Truce still broadly holding: a senior US official (Feb 2026) confirmed it 'is still in effect'; ITIC (Sep 2026) notes China 'appears to be upholding its commitments' on general licenses even as license delays/denials persist at the company level.
Alperovitch/Silverado (Sep 21 2026) assess the 'uneasy truce is likely to continue' past the summit, implying extension expected — which would push score back toward 0.

items.label: Rare-earth export license flow (0 flowing / 1 slowing / 2 frozen)
items.rationale: The regime is unambiguously case-by-case (per-shipment licences required for controlled categories; general licences confined to named producers only), new categories were added to the control list within the trailing 3 months (Jan 2026 catalogue additions remain in effect), and processing times routinely exceed 30 days (60-120 days observed for heavy-REE). All three SLOWING triggers under rubric level 1 are met; no categorical denial to an entire country or sector-wide suspension of licensing issuance meets the FROZEN threshold.
items.fact: As of mid-2026, China's MOFCOM operates a mandatory case-by-case export licensing regime for heavy-REE magnets (NdFeB with Dy/Tb, SmCo) imposed in April 2025. General licences exist but are limited to a small cohort of pre-cleared major exporters (JL MAG, San Huan, Yunsheng, first issued December 2025); they are 'not broadly available.' Processing times officially target 45 working days (~9 weeks) but in practice run 60-120 days for heavy-REE materials. The January 2026 licensing catalogue added new controls on samarium, gadolinium, and lutetium compounds. MOFCOM explicitly will not approve licences for military end-users. Trump threats of 200% tariffs in August 2026 over insufficient magnet supply confirm the slow-approval signal is market-corroborated. Sources: rare-earth-mining.com (Apr 2026), blog.gettransport.com (Jul 2026), china-briefing.com (Nov 2025 updated), certivo.com (Mar 2026), techtimes.com (May 2026), energy-solutions.co (verified 2026-08-27).

dissent.view: One supplier case study (Mainrich) cites a 23-day approval for a straightforward EV-motor civilian order, implying some commercial shipments clear faster than the 60-120 day median reported elsewhere.

Rare Earth Exchanges cites licensing approval rates below 25% for European firms (Apr 2026), which could argue for a FROZEN reading for that bilateral segment, though no formal categorical denial order has been published.

items.label: SEC central clearing on track (0 ok / 1 slipping / 2 delayed)
items.rationale: One official one-year extension was granted (Feb 2025), satisfying rubric level 1's 'official extension granted' criterion; SIFMA and IIB exemptive-relief requests pending as of Apr-May 2026 further confirm level 1. No second formal deadline extension has been announced, so level 2 is not triggered.
items.fact: The SEC formally extended compliance deadlines once (Release 34-102487, Feb 25 2025): cash to Dec 31 2026, repo to Jun 30 2027. As of the SEC Commissioner Uyeda August 2026 statement (sec.gov, Aug 7 2026), those remain the operative deadlines with no second extension, but SIFMA exemptive-relief requests (inter-affiliate and IIB extraterritorial) were published by the SEC on Apr 17 2026 with a May 29 2026 comment deadline, and remain pending.

items.label: GPU-backed debt refinancing stress (0 none / 1 signs / 2 acute)
items.rationale: Named borrower (CoreWeave) faces a documented refinancing wall on GPU-backed debt with CDS spreads at deeply distressed levels (~855bps/50% 5yr PD) and major banks are actively offloading AI data-center debt, some at a discount — all hallmarks of rubric level 1 SIGNS. No confirmed default, distressed exchange, or failed refinancing has occurred as of the research date, so level 2 ACUTE is not warranted.
items.fact: CoreWeave (CRWV) CDS spread hit ~855bps on July 29, 2026 implying a 50% five-year default probability on its GPU-backed debt, while JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley, and SMBC were actively seeking to offload AI/data-center construction loans — some reportedly at a discount — due to concentration limits; CoreWeave carried a documented $4.2B 2026 refinancing wall on GPU-collateralized debt with depreciating collateral, though it subsequently closed an $8.5B DDTL (Q1), a $2B oversubscribed bond (May), a $1.5B bond (June), and a $2.6B DDTL 5.5 (Aug 10, 2026 SEC filing) without a confirmed default. Sources: TechTimes Jul 30 2026 (CDS); Tech Newsday/ResultSense May 6 2026 (bank offloading); eMarketer May 5 2026 (discount); Dave Friedman Substack Apr 19 2026 ($4.2B wall); SEC EDGAR Aug 10 2026 CRWV 8-K (DDTL 5.5 close).

items.label: Govt stability (0 stable / 1 fragile / 2 collapse-or-snap-election)
items.rationale: Lecornu's government is a minority coalition in a hung parliament (no working majority) that has relied on Article 49.3 and survived multiple no-confidence votes to govern — a textbook rubric-1 scenario. No dissolution or PM resignation has occurred, ruling out rubric 2; the absence of a working majority rules out rubric 0.
items.fact: The Second Lecornu minority government (formed 10 Oct 2025) is the incumbent government of France as of 17 Sep 2026. It survived multiple no-confidence votes in Jan-Feb 2026 (LFI motion on 23 Jan received 269 votes vs 288 needed; RN motion received fewer) after invoking Article 49.3 to pass the 2026 budget revenue section. Bloomberg, 17 Sep 2026, reports Lecornu is now preparing a 2027 budget bill that 'risks toppling the government just ahead of presidential elections,' confirming the government is still in office but acutely fragile. Sources: Reuters/Al Jazeera 14 Jan 2026; Euronews/Al Jazeera 23 Jan - 2 Feb 2026; Wikipedia 'Lecornu governments'; Bloomberg 17 Sep 2026.

items.label: Pension-fund leverage event, UK-2022 type (0 none / 1 stress / 2 blowup)
items.rationale: Both ESMA (June 2026) and TPR confirm LDI buffers are materially stronger (~300 bps headroom) and no margin-call episode or forced gilt selling has occurred; this maps cleanly to Rubric 0 (NONE: LDI buffers adequate, no margin stress). No regulator has flagged active liquidity stress in 2025-2026, and there is no evidence of a blowup episode.
items.fact: ESMA's June 2026 TRV article on LDI funds (ESMA50-1949966494-4208, published 23 June 2026) finds that 'the ability of funds to meet liquidity demands has improved compared to September 2022' and that the liquidity shortfall under stress declined from €9bn to €3bn (end-2024 data), driven by lower leveraged exposures and a smaller segment NAV (€113bn vs €130bn at the 2022 crisis). Concurrently, TPR's Market Oversight report confirms LDI managers have raised rate buffers to ~300 bps (vs ~150 bps pre-2022) and that daily volatility in leveraged LDI assets is now more than 50% lower than end-2021, with no margin-call episode or forced gilt selling reported in 2025-2026. Source: ESMA (https://www.esma.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2026-06/ESMA50-1949966494-4208_LDI_funds_-_recent_developments_and_methods_for_liquidity_stress_testing_0.pdf) and TPR (https://www.thepensionsregulator.gov.uk/en/document-library/research-and-analysis/market-oversight-how-well-pension-schemes-are-prepared-for-ldi-risk).

items.label: Rating action (0 stable / 1 negative outlook / 2 downgrade)
items.rationale: Two of the three major agencies (Fitch and S&P) executed outright one-notch rating cuts within the trailing 12-month window (Sept–Oct 2025), satisfying rubric band 2 (actual rating cut). Moody's additionally shifted to Negative outlook in the same window, reinforcing the most severe band.
items.fact: Fitch cut France AA- → A+ (stable outlook) on ~12 Sept 2025 (Euronews/Bloomberg); S&P cut France AA- → A+ (stable outlook) on ~17 Oct 2025 (Euronews); Moody's kept Aa3 but moved outlook to Negative on 25 Oct 2025 (France24). Fitch affirmed A+/Stable 28 Aug 2026; S&P affirmed A+ May 2026. All three cuts/outlook changes fall within trailing 12 months of 2026-09-21.

items.label: China PPI YoY (%) - large swing either way is worse
items.rationale: The rubric scores on the SIZE of the move regardless of sign; at +3.8% YoY China PPI is a notably positive print representing a sharp cost-push inflation signal that exports input-cost pressure globally, well above the near-zero baseline of early 2026. This is a material positive-side price-spillover reading.
items.fact: China PPI for industrial products increased 3.8% year-on-year in August 2026, per NBS data released 9 September 2026 (corroborated by People's Daily en.people.cn/n3/2026/0909/c90000-20497638.html and Vantage Markets vantagemarkets.com/market-news/china-cpi-ppi-august-energy-prices-september-9-2026/; prior month July was +3.5% per NBS official release stats.gov.cn/english/PressRelease/202608/t20260810_1965017.html).

items.label: US domestic RE producer blacklist (0 none / 1 entity-specific ban / 2 sector-wide ban)
items.rationale: Two named US rare-earth producers (MP Materials and USA Rare Earth) are explicitly listed in a firm-specific MOFCOM announcement; the restriction targets 10 individually named companies, not a categorical class of US rare-earth producers or all US dual-use recipients, mapping squarely to rubric score 1. No evidence of a sector-wide or categorical ban (score 2) exists.
items.fact: On 22 June 2026, China MOFCOM issued Announcement No. 23 of 2026 adding 10 named US entities to its export-control list, explicitly including MP Materials Corp. and USA Rare Earth, Inc., alongside eight defence/aerospace firms (Red Cat Holdings, Teal Drones, Aveox, Oshkosh Defense, L3Harris Maritime Services, and others). The ban prohibits Chinese exporters from shipping dual-use items to the named entities and bars any third-country transfer of Chinese-origin dual-use items to them, effective immediately. Source: MOFCOM Announcement No. 23 of 2026, corroborated by Benchmark Mineral Intelligence (25 Jun 2026), Bloomberg (22 Jun 2026), Arnold & Porter advisory (2 Jul 2026), and SMM/metal.com (22 Jun 2026). Benchmark explicitly characterises the measure as 'entity-specific rather than a blanket restriction on rare earth exports to the US.'

s1_basis_trade.label: Hidden leverage in US government bonds
s1_basis_trade.gist: Hedge funds borrow heavily to trade US government bonds; if that trade unwinds fast it can freeze the market everyone treats as safe.

s2_japan.label: Japan's rates and the global cash carry trade
s2_japan.gist: Cheap Japanese money has funded bets worldwide for years; as Japan's interest rates rise, pulling that money home can ripple through global markets.

s3_private_credit.label: Private lending you can't see into
s3_private_credit.gist: A fast-growing pile of loans sits outside the banks with little public disclosure, so stress there is hard to spot until it is already large.

s4_dev_debt.label: Debt stress in developing countries
s4_dev_debt.gist: Many poorer nations owe more than they can comfortably repay; a wave of defaults can spread and pull in their lenders.

s5_china_deflation.label: China's prices spilling into the world
s5_china_deflation.gist: Big swings in China's factory prices - falling or rising - get exported to everyone else as cheaper goods or higher input costs.

s6_rare_earths.label: Rare-earth minerals used as a weapon
s6_rare_earths.gist: China controls most of the world's rare-earth processing and is now restricting it, squeezing US defense and high-tech manufacturing.

s7_stablecoins.label: Crypto dollars and US government debt
s7_stablecoins.gist: Stablecoins must hold US Treasuries as backing, so their rapid growth - or a sudden wobble - now feeds straight back into the government-debt market.

s8_ai_capex.label: The AI spending boom
s8_ai_capex.gist: Enormous borrowing to build AI data centers is racing ahead of the revenue meant to justify it, concentrating the risk in a few giant companies.

s9_cre.label: Commercial real estate and small banks
s9_cre.gist: Half-empty offices and loans coming due strain the regional banks that hold them - a slow-burning credit risk.

s10_france.label: France and eurozone stability
s10_france.gist: A politically gridlocked, heavily indebted France is the soft spot that could reopen broader euro-area stress.

s11_consumer_debt.label: Household debt strain
s11_consumer_debt.gist: Rising late payments on car loans and buy-now-pay-later show households stretching - an early warning on consumer health.

s12_gold_dedollar.label: Gold and moving away from the dollar
s12_gold_dedollar.gist: Central banks stockpiling gold and building non-dollar payment systems slowly chip away at the dollar's dominance.

s13_insurance.label: Insurers pulling back
s13_insurance.gist: As disaster losses climb, insurers raise prices or quit whole regions, leaving homes and assets exposed.

s14_pensions.label: Pensions and an aging population
s14_pensions.gist: Aging populations and underfunded pensions strain public budgets; leveraged pension funds can also break in a sudden rate shock, as the UK saw in 2022.

s15_ai_power.label: AI's strain on the power grid
s15_ai_power.gist: AI data centers need more electricity than the grid can quickly supply, triggering curtailments, building moratoria, and multi-year connection queues.

s16_copper.label: Copper for electrification
s16_copper.gist: Electrifying everything needs far more copper than mines can deliver, and major mine outages are tightening supply further.

s17_water.label: Water as a hidden constraint
s17_water.gist: Droughts and shrinking reservoirs threaten chip factories, farms, and power generation - an underpriced input with no substitute.

s18_food_fertilizer.label: Food and fertilizer supply
s18_food_fertilizer.gist: Export curbs and shipping disruptions to fertilizer raise the risk of higher food prices down the line.

s19_lithography.label: The chipmaking chokepoint
s19_lithography.gist: The most advanced chips depend on one Dutch tool-maker and Taiwan's factories; any disruption there hits the entire tech economy.

s20_sea_lanes.label: Shipping lanes and undersea cables
s20_sea_lanes.gist: Key straits like Hormuz and the undersea cables carrying the internet are vulnerable chokepoints for global trade and data.

s21_clearinghouses.label: The financial system's plumbing
s21_clearinghouses.gist: Clearinghouses sit at the center of every market; if one seized up under stress, it would jam trading everywhere at once.

playbook.disclaimer: Educational cause-and-effect only - how stress like this has historically moved through the system. Nothing here is investment advice or a prediction.

s1_basis_trade.mechanism: A rates shock forces highly leveraged government-bond arbitrage positions to unwind at once: margin calls trigger forced Treasury selling, liquidity in the world's benchmark market evaporates, and everything priced off it reprices.
benefits: cash and short-term bills through the panic
long-term government bonds AFTER central-bank intervention
s1_basis_trade.watch: The funding-spread and bond-volatility rows above; the historical pivot was the central bank announcing a backstop facility.
s1_basis_trade.trap: In past episodes the 'safe' asset itself fell first - forced sellers sell what they can - so the flight-to-safety instinct lost money until the intervention.

s2_japan.mechanism: Surging Japanese yields pull decades of cheap yen funding home: the yen spikes on repatriation, and leveraged positions worldwide that were financed in yen get liquidated together - hitting high-momentum equities and emerging markets hardest.
benefits: Japanese banks and insurers as rates normalize
s2_japan.watch: The 30-year JGB row above (live official feed) and the yen; past unwinds announced themselves through the currency.
s2_japan.trap: Historical carry unwinds were violent but brief - the 2024 episode round-tripped within days; the durable shift was in Japanese financials, not the panic.

s3_private_credit.mechanism: One honest markdown forces everyone's marks: investor withdrawals hit gates, gated funds fire-sell into an illiquid market, and lending to mid-sized companies contracts just as they need to refinance.
bleeds: private-credit vehicles trading below stated asset value
benefits: holders of dry powder buying discounted credit afterwards
public high-quality credit as the flight destination
s3_private_credit.watch: The default-rate and redemption-gate rows above; public high-yield spreads are the honest proxy for hidden marks.
s3_private_credit.trap: Opacity means the repricing arrives as a sudden gap, not a trend - by the time it is public, the move has largely happened.

s4_dev_debt.mechanism: A cluster of sovereign defaults - not one - overwhelms the restructuring machinery: redemptions from emerging-market debt funds force indiscriminate selling of strong and weak credits alike, and stress spreads through common creditors.
benefits: and historically the buyers of defaulted debt after restructuring - among the best-documented recoveries in fixed income
s4_dev_debt.watch: The new-IMF-programs row above and the dollar's strength, which is usually the upstream cause.
s4_dev_debt.trap: Index diversification means one or two defaults barely register; the systemic wave this story warns of is exactly what official bailouts exist to prevent.

s5_china_deflation.mechanism: Deepening factory-gate deflation is exported as cheaper goods, compressing margins for competing producers everywhere - unless Beijing's stimulus response whipsaws the pressure into a sudden commodity and China-equity rebound.
benefits: long-term bonds in the deflation leg
Chinese equities and industrial metals in the stimulus leg
s5_china_deflation.watch: The producer-price row above and any stimulus announcement - the two legs point opposite directions.
s5_china_deflation.trap: Policy whipsaw: historically every stimulus rumor violently reversed the deflation trade within days.

s6_rare_earths.mechanism: Export restrictions tighten into denial: magnet and heavy-rare-earth supply to defense, vehicle, and robotics manufacturers halts, panic stockpiling begins, and processing capacity outside China re-rates from commodity business to strategic asset.
bleeds: vehicle and defense production schedules in the short run
s6_rare_earths.watch: The license-flow, blacklist, and ex-China premium rows above - the premium is the market's own severity gauge.
s6_rare_earths.trap: Historically these moves reversed as fast as they started on any truce headline, and diversified funds in the space often hold the Chinese producers too.

s7_stablecoins.mechanism: A run on a major stablecoin forces its reserves - tens of billions in short-term government debt - to liquidate within days, briefly dislocating the bill market while the crypto ecosystem's dollar rails seize and leveraged positions cascade.
benefits: historically the surviving issuer gained lasting market share after each depeg scare
s7_stablecoins.watch: The live peg-deviation and supply rows above (updated daily from the aggregator) - past runs announced themselves in the peg first.
s7_stablecoins.trap: Crypto markets have a long history of face-ripping rebounds inside downtrends; past episodes punished conviction in both directions.

s8_ai_capex.mechanism: The debt-financed buildout meets a revenue shortfall: one credit event at a leveraged data-center operator reprices all AI-adjacent borrowing, capital-spending guidance gets cut, chip orders fall, and power-demand forecasts deflate - the whole complex moves together because it was funded together.
bleeds: power producers priced on AI demand
benefits: and - the dot-com lesson - the post-bust survivors compounded for a decade
s8_ai_capex.watch: The capex-gap, revenue-gap, and refinancing rows above; credit stress historically led equity repricing.
s8_ai_capex.trap: Bubbles run longer than solvency: betting against this one early has been the era's classic ruin trade, which is why timing signals matter more than valuation.

s9_cre.mechanism: Office refinancing failures cluster into bank failures: deposit flight spreads to lookalike regional lenders, credit to small business contracts, and commercial-property marks finally reflect reality.
benefits: the largest banks via deposit inflows
and historically the whole sector rebounded within days of a backstop
s9_cre.watch: The bank-failure and office-delinquency rows above and the official problem-bank list.
s9_cre.trap: The 2023 backstop bottomed the sector in 48 hours - the policy response, not the failure, was the historical turning point.

s10_france.mechanism: Fiscal paralysis pushes French borrowing costs through crisis thresholds: banks holding the government's own bonds absorb the losses, the sovereign-bank doom loop reawakens, and stress spreads across euro-area borrowing costs.
bleeds: other high-debt euro members through contagion
benefits: and non-euro safe havens in every euro crisis
s10_france.watch: The OAT-Bund spread row above (live feed) - it is the market's single-number verdict on this story.
s10_france.trap: The central bank: euro-breakup positioning has been ruined repeatedly by ECB backstops built precisely for this scenario.

s11_consumer_debt.mechanism: Subprime stress spreads upward: rising late payments become charge-offs, lenders tighten, discretionary spending cracks, and the weakness travels from consumer lenders to retailers to the broad economy.
benefits: trade-down retailers in every past consumer squeeze
s11_consumer_debt.watch: The subprime-delinquency and BNPL rows above; the staples-versus-discretionary ratio is the market's own recession gauge.
s11_consumer_debt.trap: Lenders provision ahead of losses - their shares historically bottomed while delinquencies were still rising.

s12_gold_dedollar.mechanism: A reserve-weaponization event accelerates the slow shift: central banks swap dollar assets for gold at a faster pace, marginal foreign demand for government debt weakens, and the metal gains a structural, price-insensitive buyer.
bleeds: long-term government bonds via lost foreign demand
benefits: gold above all - the current central-bank buying era is the live example - plus non-dollar safe havens
s12_gold_dedollar.watch: The reserve-share row above (quarterly official data) and central-bank purchase reports.
s12_gold_dedollar.trap: This is measured in decades, not events - and gold miners have historically lagged the metal itself across full cycles.

s13_insurance.mechanism: A mega-catastrophe season collides with insurers already exiting exposed regions: property becomes uninsurable, collateral values fall, and the stress transmits to mortgages, regional lenders, and state backstops.
bleeds: property values and lenders in exposed regions
benefits: historically reinsurers AFTER the event as pricing hardened
and catastrophe-linked debt yields for risk-bearers
s13_insurance.watch: The insurer-exit and catastrophe-loss rows above plus the season's forecasts.
s13_insurance.trap: Positioning before the event absorbs the loss; the well-documented historical pattern favored the post-event hard market.

s14_pensions.mechanism: A rate spike forces leveraged pension strategies into collateral calls: they dump whatever is liquid, the selling pushes yields higher still, and the spiral continues until a central bank steps in - the UK lived this in 2022.
bleeds: long-term government bonds during the spiral itself
retirees' security in the slow version
benefits: whoever provided liquidity at the intervention - the 2022 central-bank entry marked the exact bottom - and retirement insurers structurally as rates rose
s14_pensions.watch: The funded-ratio row above (live monthly feed) and long-bond volatility.
s14_pensions.trap: Identical to the basis trade: buying the falling 'safe' asset before the intervention caught knives for days.

s15_ai_power.mechanism: Data-center demand outruns the grid so badly that curtailments, connection queues, and building moratoria stall the buildout - rising household bills turn it political, and the constraint moves from engineering to consent.
bleeds: utilities caught between regulators and demand
benefits: and nuclear/gas capacity - though see the trap
s15_ai_power.watch: The interconnection-wait and moratoria rows above and capacity-auction prices.
s15_ai_power.trap: The famous version of this trade assumes the buildout CONTINUES; this story's actual blow-up - moratoria stopping it - points the opposite way for the same names.

s16_copper.mechanism: A structural deficit meets a supply shock - a major mine closure removes years of planned supply - and the metal prices high enough to ration demand, raising costs for every grid, vehicle, and data-center project simultaneously.
benefits: producing miners with volume to sell
s16_copper.watch: The mine-disruption and deficit rows above and exchange inventory levels.
s16_copper.trap: The political risk that causes the shocks sits inside the producers themselves - the closed mine may be the one you were counting on.

s17_water.mechanism: Severe drought hits a chip hub, a farm belt, and cooling-dependent power at once: an unpriced input becomes a binding constraint, cutting industrial output regionally and feeding into food prices.
benefits: historically crop prices in drought years
s17_water.watch: The reservoir and drought rows above (live official feed for the largest US reservoir).
s17_water.trap: There is no pure play - broad 'water' funds are mostly global industrials, while the shock is local; the honest effects are second-order.

s18_food_fertilizer.mechanism: Fertilizer export restrictions cut application in poorer countries, next season's yields fall, grain prices spike, and food inflation becomes social and fiscal stress in import-dependent nations - looping back into the developing-world debt story.
benefits: fertilizer producers in every past squeeze
s18_food_fertilizer.watch: The FAO food-price row above (live feed) and the export-curb indicator.
s18_food_fertilizer.trap: Fertilizer stress historically reversed violently when curbs lifted, taking back most of the move.

s19_lithography.mechanism: Conflict or blockade around Taiwan stops the fabs that make nearly all leading-edge chips: every electronics supply chain seizes within a quarter, and the shock is large enough that markets themselves may not function normally.
bleeds: and anything with a chip in it
s19_lithography.watch: The tension and export-control rows above; false-alarm cycles have historically outnumbered real escalations many times over.
s19_lithography.trap: In the true scenario, settlement and market access are themselves at risk - analysis that assumes functioning markets may not apply.

s20_sea_lanes.mechanism: A chokepoint closes - this board just watched Hormuz do it - and shipping rates, war-risk insurance, and energy prices spike together while longer reroutes quietly shrink effective global capacity; cable cuts do the same for data.
s20_sea_lanes.watch: The live strait-transit feed and cable-incident rows above.
s20_sea_lanes.trap: This board's own history shows it: reopening headlines crushed the shipping move within days - persistence of the disruption was everything.

s21_clearinghouses.mechanism: A major member defaults into a volatile market and the clearinghouse's loss waterfall activates: surviving members face assessments and de-risk simultaneously, margin requirements spiral procyclically, and the plumbing everyone assumed away becomes the crisis itself.
benefits: almost nothing leveraged - which is the honest answer; cash
and physical assets have no counterparty
s21_clearinghouses.watch: The clearing-mandate rollout row above and any clearinghouse margin announcements.
s21_clearinghouses.trap: The deepest on the board: in a true clearing failure, a winning derivative position may itself not pay out.

context.intro: The famous dials, for contrast. These are the most-watched macro gauges in the world - shown here so you can compare them with this tracker's structural lens. They are not part of the score. When they disagree with the gauge above, that divergence is the story: markets price these continuously, while the risks this tracker follows are the kind markets historically ignored until they ruptured.

items.label: VIX
items.note: Expected US stock-market volatility - the most-watched fear gauge. Calm markets usually sit below ~20.

items.label: 10y-2y curve
items.note: 10-year minus 2-year Treasury yield. A negative (inverted) reading has historically preceded US recessions - with long and variable lags.

items.label: High-yield spread
items.note: The extra yield markets demand to lend to risky companies - the market's own price of credit stress. Calm is roughly below ~4.

items.label: Chicago Fed NFCI
items.note: The Chicago Fed's broad financial-conditions index across money, debt, and equity markets. Negative = looser (calmer) than average.

items.label: Unemployment
items.note: The US unemployment rate - the classic real-economy dial, updated monthly.
